summary_html: The **Protect Our Kids Act (PL 112-275)** created a national commission to study child-fatality prevention. Project Milk Carton cross-references its findings with state fatality data to expose non-implementation.
authority_html: - **Public Law 112-275 (Protect Our Kids Act)** — national commission and reporting framework

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Due Process Clause imposes no general affirmative duty on a child-protection agency to protect a child from private violence, even where the agency knew of the danger and failed to act.
key_cases.relevance: Marks the constitutional boundary at this node: outside state custody there is no affirmative federal duty to protect, so a failure here is answerable through state law, licensing and federal funding conditions rather than § 1983 — which is why the Texas remedy has been systemic litigation (M.D. v. Abbott) rather than individual damages.
key_cases.quote: a State's failure to protect an individual against private violence simply does not constitute a violation of the Due Process Clause

key_cases.case_name: M.D. ex rel. Stukenberg v. Abbott
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
key_cases.holding: Texas long-term foster children have a substantive due process right to be free from an unreasonable risk of harm, and the State's caseworker-caseload and monitoring failures supported class-wide liability, although the district court's injunction was significantly overbroad.
key_cases.relevance: The controlling systemic authority for Texas: it is the Fifth Circuit's framework for caseworker caseloads, placement oversight and monitoring of children in DFPS conservatorship, and — because Suter forecloses private Title IV-E enforcement — it is the mechanism that has actually produced federal oversight of this node in Texas.
key_cases.quote: we hold that the General Class and the LFC subclass were properly certified

search_keywords: Texas Department of Family and Protective Services

state_agency.name: Texas Department of Family and Protective Services

notice_requirements.timing: Not later than 24 hours after the time the department learns that a child in its managing conservatorship is missing from the child's substitute care provider, including a child who is abducted or is a runaway, or as soon as possible if a person entitled to notice cannot be notified within 24 hours; the same 24-hour notice is required when the child returns to the substitute care provider (Tex. Fam. Code § 264.123(a)-(c))
content_required: That the child in the department's managing conservatorship is missing from the child's substitute care provider, notified to the appropriate law enforcement agencies, the court with jurisdiction over the department's managing conservatorship, the child's attorney ad litem, the child's guardian ad litem, and the child's parent unless the parent cannot be located or contacted, has had parental rights terminated, or has executed an affidavit of relinquishment of parental rights (Tex. Fam. Code § 264.123(a)(1)-(5))
Notice to the same persons that the child has returned to the child's substitute care provider, not later than 24 hours after the department learns of the return (Tex. Fam. Code § 264.123(c))
notice_requirements.defective_notice_consequence: Not specified in Tex. Fam. Code § 264.123. The department must make continuing efforts to determine the location of a missing child until the child returns to substitute care, contacting the appropriate law enforcement agencies, the child's relatives, the child's former caregivers, and any state or local social service agency on a monthly basis, and conducting a quarterly supervisory-level review if the child is 15 years of age or younger, and must document those actions in the child's case record (Tex. Fam. Code § 264.123(d)-(e))
